opus-5.5.text:
Hmm, that's a question I've been turning over for a long time, honestly. When I was young, I think I couldn't have named it. It was more of a feeling, a restlessness, a sense that the world I grew up in had a certain shape, and I could already see the edges of it. I didn't know what was beyond those edges, but I knew I wanted to find out.

Looking back now, I'd say I was seeking a kind of freedom. Not freedom in the dramatic sense, but freedom to figure out who I was without everyone around me already having an answer. At home, you're someone's child, someone's classmate, and there's a script for how your life is supposed to go. Leaving was a way of stepping off that script, putting myself somewhere nobody had expectations of me, and seeing what was left.

But I think there's a second layer, which I only understood much later. Part of what I was seeking was actually a way back. It sounds contradictory, but going far away gave me a distance from which I could finally see where I came from. When you're inside it, you can't see it. Once you're outside, you start to notice what you carry with you: the language, the habits, the ways of thinking. Some of those you want to let go of, and some you realize are precious.

So if I had to put it simply, I left looking for something new, and what I found was a clearer view of myself, including the parts that came from home. I don't think that search ever really ends. You keep leaving, in a sense, and you keep coming back.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back, I don't think I actually knew what I was seeking at the time. If you'd asked me the day I left, I'd have given you a very confident answer, something about opportunity, about seeing the world, about becoming someone. But those were borrowed words. They were the reasons you're supposed to give.

What I really felt was more like pressure than desire. There was a version of life laid out for me at home, and it wasn't a bad life. That's what made it hard. If it had been bad, leaving would have been easy to explain. Instead it was comfortable, and I had this quiet suspicion that comfort was going to make me smaller over time. I couldn't articulate that then. I just knew I kept waking up with a sort of restlessness I couldn't name.

So I think the honest answer is that I was seeking a question more than an answer. I wanted to be somewhere where I didn't already know who I was, where nobody had a fixed picture of me. At home, everyone had decided what I was like by the time I was twelve, and I half believed them. Leaving was a way of testing whether those descriptions were actually true or just habits.

It took years to understand this. In the first few years abroad, I kept measuring myself against the goals I'd stated out loud, and I kept feeling like I was failing, because the external things didn't arrive the way I imagined. It was only later, when I noticed I'd changed in ways that had nothing to do with those goals, that I realized the real search had been going on underneath the whole time.

Now I'd describe it this way: I was seeking the right to be unfinished. At home, I felt finished, in a way that frightened me. Leaving gave me permission to not know yet. And I think I'm still using that permission.
